  "question": "What does it mean that every transaction can be checked by anyone?",
  "answer": "On most public blockchains, the full transaction history is stored openly, and anyone can read it without permission. You don't need an account or a bank to look it up. You can check that a payment was sent, when it was confirmed, how much moved, and whether the network accepted it. Because every participant keeps or can verify the same ledger, no single company or intermediary has to be trusted to report the truth.",
  "key_points": [
    "Public ledger: Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana, and similar networks publish every confirmed transaction, including sender address, recipient address, amount, fees, and timestamp.",
    "Independent verification: Anyone can recheck cryptographic signatures and consensus rules, so a node operator doesn't have to take another party's word for a balance.",
    "Permanent record: Confirmed transactions are very hard to alter or delete, which makes the history auditable over time.",
    "Pseudonymity, not anonymity: Transactions are tied to addresses rather than names. Activity is visible, but identity is only revealed if someone links an address to a real person."
  ],
  "examples": [
    "Block explorers: Etherscan (Ethereum), Solscan (Solana), Mempool.space and Blockchair (Bitcoin), and Blockscout (open-source explorer used by many EVM chains).",
    "Full nodes: Bitcoin Core and Geth let users download and verify the entire chain themselves instead of relying on a third-party explorer.",
    "Chain analytics: Chainalysis, Elliptic, and TRM Labs use public data to trace fund flows, which is used for compliance and investigations."
  ],
  "caveats": [
    "Transparency is not the same as privacy. Public activity can be analyzed, and address reuse or exchange deposits can expose identities.",
    "Privacy-focused networks limit visibility. Monero hides sender, receiver, and amount by default, and Zcash offers shielded transactions.",
    "Permissioned blockchains such as Hyperledger Fabric and R3 Corda restrict who can see transaction data, so 'anyone can check' does not apply to them.",
    "Because records are permanent, errors such as sending to a wrong address cannot be reversed by the network itself."

{
  "query": "How do the project terms and final payouts get enforced if no one can override them?",
  "answer": "I don't have verified, current technical documentation on SpaceM's specific payout or enforcement architecture, so I can't confirm how its terms are enforced. In most Web3 systems that claim no one can override payouts, enforcement comes from one or more of the following mechanisms:\n\n1. Immutable smart contracts: Terms and payout logic are encoded on-chain (for example on Ethereum, Solana, or Base). Once deployed, the code executes automatically when conditions are met. Payouts occur without an intermediary deciding to release funds.\n2. Escrow and vesting contracts: Funds are locked in a contract and released on a schedule or on verifiable conditions. Examples include Sablier and Hedgey for token streaming and vesting, and Superfluid for continuous payment flows.\n3. Multisig or timelock governance: Even where admin keys exist, changes may require multiple signers (Safe, formerly Gnosis Safe) and a delay (OpenZeppelin TimelockController). This makes overrides visible and slow rather than impossible.\n4. External oracles or adjudication: When payout conditions depend on off-chain events, enforcement relies on oracles such as Chainlink or UMA's optimistic oracle, or on dispute resolution systems such as Kleros.\n5. Off-chain legal agreements: Some projects pair on-chain code with contracts enforceable in courts. This is common when the code alone cannot represent the terms.\n\nImportant caveat: \"No one can override\" claims are often weaker than they sound. Common gaps include upgradeable proxy contracts where an admin can change the logic, pause functions, admin keys that can drain or freeze funds, oracle manipulation, and bugs. Enforcement is only as strong as the contract's actual admin controls, which you can check directly.",
  "key_points": [
    "Whether payouts are truly unoverridable depends on the specific contract: check for proxy/upgrade patterns, owner or admin roles, pause functions, and emergency withdrawals.",
    "Immutable contracts with no admin functions give the strongest guarantee, but they cannot correct bugs or handle unforeseen situations.",
    "Timelocks and multisigs reduce but do not eliminate override risk.",
    "Off-chain conditions introduce trust in oracles or adjudicators.",
    "Audits (for example by Trail of Bits, OpenZeppelin, or Certora) and verified source code on block explorers are the practical way to confirm these properties."
  ],

    "Safe (multisig custody and governance)",
    "Chainlink and UMA (oracles for conditional payouts)",
    "Kleros (decentralized dispute resolution)",
    "Unlock Protocol (on-chain subscriptions and access payments)"
  ],

    "SpaceM's official documentation, whitepaper, or terms of service",
    "Deployed contract addresses and verified source code on Etherscan or the relevant block explorer",
    "Audit reports and their stated admin-key findings",

Immutable smart contracts: Terms and payout logic are encoded on-chain (for example on Ethereum, Solana, or Base). Once deployed, the code executes automatically when conditions are met. Payouts occur without an intermediary deciding to release funds.\n2. Escrow and vesting contracts: Funds are locked in a contract and released on a schedule or on verifiable conditions. Examples include Sablier and Hedgey for token streaming and vesting, and Superfluid for continuous payment flows.\n3. Multisig or timelock governance: Even where admin keys exist, changes may require multiple signers (Safe, formerly Gnosis Safe) and a delay (OpenZeppelin TimelockController). This makes overrides visible and slow rather than impossible.\n4. External oracles or adjudication: When payout conditions depend on off-chain events, enforcement relies on oracles such as Chainlink or UMA's optimistic oracle, or on dispute resolution systems such as Kleros.\n5. Off-chain legal agreements: Some projects pair on-chain code with contracts enforceable in courts. This is common when the code alone cannot represent the terms.\n\nImportant caveat: \"No one can override\" claims are often weaker than they sound. Common gaps include upgradeable proxy contracts where an admin can change the logic, pause functions, admin keys that can drain or freeze funds, oracle manipulation, and bugs.
